title: Segment then Splat: Unified 3D Open-Vocabulary Segmentation via Gaussian Splatting
provenance_note: The exact inspected current paper PDF is identified by its SHA-256. The current author README explicitly links this arXiv revision and qualifies initialization as To be verified. summary: The current release retains small-mask encoding, correspondence, pruning and query discrepancies. Threshold filtering also does not ensure disjoint pixel ownership; the separate Boolean-IoU allegation remains rejected.

problems.title: The small-mask byte encoding removes foreground before supervision
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, Eq. (8), PDF p. 6; released scene/dataset_readers.py, lines 162–175.
claim: Section 3.4, Eq. (8), PDF p. 6, includes small-object supervision. Released scene/dataset_readers.py, lines 162–175, thresholds a Pillow mode-L mask by whether each pixel exceeds \(128\). utils/general_utils.py, lines 23–25, divides the resulting bytes by \(255\), and utils/camera_utils.py, lines 46–48, applies threshold \(0.5\). train.py skips small masks that become empty.
analysis: The mode-L threshold stores foreground bytes as \(1\), not \(255\). Dividing by \(255\) therefore gives \(1/255\), below the next threshold \(0.5\). Foreground inputs such as \(129\) and \(255\) are erased before the small-mask supervision loop. This is deterministic for the inspected reader, while its role in historical table-producing runs remains unidentified.
result: The current byte reader deterministically erases small foreground; exposure in historical scene training and the corresponding mIoU change are unknown.
repair: Preserve the byte convention by returning \(255\) for foreground and \(0\) otherwise before division by \(255\), or use a consistently Boolean path.
problems.impact_rationale: The current byte reader deterministically erases small foreground; exposure in historical scene training and the corresponding mIoU change are unknown.
problems.existing_correction_status: A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Initialization does not consistently preserve frame, granularity, and object identity
claim: Section 3.3, p. 5, assigns an object ID using the visible point’s mask region and merges duplicate object tracks using the means of their Gaussian centers and colors; Equation (4) describes that distance. The following three subcases concern the released helpers/object_specific_initialization.py. They are separate failure mechanisms within one correspondence invariant. The README’s existing To be verified status applies directly to this helper.
analysis: Three distinct identity mechanisms fail: a training-only frame counter indexes masks loaded for all frames; small-object means use middle-object membership; and merged masks are renumbered while Gaussian IDs retain old labels. Each can associate valid geometry with the wrong supervision independently of mask encoding.

With sorted frames \(0,1,2\), only \(0,2\) used for training, the second accepted observation reads frame \(1\) masks because the counter advances only for training frames. A point owned by object \(0\) in both actual training frames can therefore be assigned object \(1\).

For small groups with centers \[0.005,10.005,20.005,-9.795\], nested into middle groups \(\{0,1\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\), the wrong selector compares middle centers \(5.005,5.105\). Colors \[(0,0,0),(2,2,2),(1,1,1),(3,3,3)\] yield implemented distance \(0.1+20\sqrt3/255<0.5\), whereas the intended first two small groups give \(10+40\sqrt3/255>0.5\).
Merging initial IDs \(0,1\) among \(0,1,2\) leaves point IDs \((0,0,2)\), but compacted mask folders are \(0,1\). The surviving last object thus has incompatible identifiers.
result: The inspected correspondence helper violates those source-level identity contracts. Its own README marks it ‘To be verified’; this is affirmative reason not to infer that the published experiments used the same incomplete helper.
repair: Align frame keys, select membership from the matching granularity, and apply one explicit merge/reindex map to both masks and Gaussian IDs.
problems.impact_rationale: Three current helper outputs violate frame or object identity, while the author README explicitly marks initialization unverified.
problems.existing_correction_status: A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The Gaussian persistence loop cancels every pruning proposal
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, PDF p. 6; released scene/gaussian_model.py, GaussianModel.densify_and_prune, lines 387–421.
claim: Section 3.4, PDF p. 6, protects an object against complete pruning. Released scene/gaussian_model.py, GaussianModel.densify_and_prune, lines 387–421, clears an object's pruning flags when its original count is below \(1000\). Otherwise it compares that count with a new sum over the same unfiltered object membership and clears the flags when they agree.
analysis: The persistence loop compares each object's original count with a fresh sum over that same unfiltered membership, an identity. It consequently clears every nonempty object's pruning flags, even for \(1001\) points proposing one deletion with \(1000\) survivors. The loop does not implement a test of the number of proposed survivors.
result: The current membership-count identity cancels all valid scalar-ID pruning proposals; its full-scene memory and accuracy effects remain unmeasured.
repair: Count proposed survivors \(r_g=\sum_{j\in S_g}(1-P_j)\) and explicitly enforce the selected minimum. Comparing the original membership count with itself cannot detect extinction.
problems.impact_rationale: The current membership-count identity cancels all valid scalar-ID pruning proposals; its full-scene memory and accuracy effects remain unmeasured.
problems.existing_correction_status: A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The query helper changes both the score and eligible object levels
problems.source_location: Granularity definitions, PDF p. 4; Section 3.5, Eqs. (9)–(11), PDF p. 7.
claim: Section 3.5, Equations (9)–(11), p. 7, averages per-view object embeddings, embeds the text query, and selects the object with maximal cosine similarity. The method also introduces large, middle, and small granularities on p. 4.

In helpers/evaluation.py, extract_CLIP_embeddings at line 72 calls model.encode_image and averages the resulting features. calculate_IoU calls model.encode_text at line 143 and forms matrix products at lines 148–149, with no normalization of these mean embeddings. The small-level similarity and selection are commented out at lines 150 and \(156\)–158. The final branch at lines 165–170 compares only large and middle candidates.
analysis: For query \((1,0)\), raw dot products rank object \((2,2)\) above \((1,0)\), with scores \(2\) and \(1\). Cosines reverse that order, giving \(1/\sqrt2\) and \(1\). Unnormalized averaged image embeddings therefore do not implement the stated cosine ranking. Independently, omitting small-level candidates prevents selecting a legitimate small-level winner.
result: Unnormalized means can reverse cosine rankings and small candidates are excluded, without a measured benchmark-query failure rate.
repair: The proposed correction normalizes final nonzero object means and query, and evaluates the explicitly declared candidate granularities with identities attached.
problems.impact_rationale: Unnormalized means can reverse cosine rankings and small candidates are excluded, without a measured benchmark-query failure rate.

problems.title: IoU threshold filtering alone does not guarantee unique pixel ownership
claim: The source describes IoU-based mask filtering as ensuring one object per pixel at a granularity.
analysis: Masks \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) and \(\{3,4,5,6\}\) overlap at one pixel but have IoU \(1/7<0.5\), so both survive the stated threshold. Filtering by overlap magnitude does not guarantee disjoint pixel ownership. A later single-valued assignment also does not make the input masks themselves disjoint.
result: Supported scope qualification of the uniqueness guarantee; no arbitrary semantic overlap-resolution rule is invented.
assumptions: Bounded to the stated source/component; no published-run provenance inferred.
problems.impact_rationale: An overlap threshold below total disjointness cannot imply unique ownership; no untested semantic resolution policy is supplied.

impact_rationale: Current source retains local implementation discrepancies, with the author explicitly qualifying initialization as unverified. No reconstructed scene or corrected benchmark result links them to central empirical conclusions.
